issues.legal_issue: Special legislation governing a uniquely important religious institution does not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality merely because it treats that institution differently from other institutions.
material_facts: The legislation applied specifically to a temple that the State described as unique in the region and of national importance.
The temple attracted large numbers of pilgrims from across the country and had assets and complex practices that were not comparable to those of other temples in the region.
The challenger did not deny the State’s account of the temple’s distinctive importance.
issues.conclusion: The temple could be treated as a class by itself, so the special legislation did not violate Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 permits different treatment where a person or institution has special circumstances or characteristics that distinguish it from others. The Court relied on Tilkayat Shri Govindlalji v. State of Rajasthan, which held that a law may constitutionally apply to a single individual treated as a class by himself where special circumstances justify it.

predicates.special_legislation_challenged: A party challenges legislation that applies specially to one institution as unequal treatment.
predicates.institution_has_distinctive_importance: The institution has distinctive importance or circumstances that set it apart from other institutions of its kind.
predicates.other_institutions_are_not_comparable: The institutions said to be treated differently do not have characteristics comparable to those of the specially regulated institution.
predicates.institution_attracts_widespread_public_a: The institution attracts substantial public attention or participation beyond its local community.

issues.definition: When special legislation is challenged and the institution has distinctive importance, its distinctiveness from comparable institutions or its widespread public significance permits differential treatment.

issues.legal_issue: Replacing a person’s sole management role over institutional property with a management body does not constitute an acquisition of that role or property where the role carries no beneficial enjoyment of the property.
material_facts: The challenger’s predecessor had held the sole management role, and the legislation transferred management to a committee.
The challenger became the committee’s chairperson.
The management role carried no beneficial enjoyment of the temple’s property, and the State did not acquire the extinguished office or vest its rights in itself.
issues.conclusion: The transfer of management did not violate Articles 19(1)(f) or 31(2).
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that ending one functionary’s management role and creating another body to administer property is not an acquisition of the former office or its rights for the purpose of Article 31(2). It relied on Tilkayat Shri Govindlalji v. State of Rajasthan. It also held that the management right in this case was not property for Article 19(1)(f), because it carried no beneficial enjoyment of property.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_management_t: A party in a constitutional challenge objects to legislation transferring sole management of an institution to another body.
predicates.sole_management_role_replaced_by_collect: The legislation ends one person’s sole management role and assigns management to a collective body.
predicates.management_role_carries_no_beneficial_pr: The management role does not give its holder beneficial enjoyment of the institution’s property.
predicates.former_manager_retains_participation_in_: The former manager remains a participant in the body that replaces the former management arrangement.

issues.definition: A management transfer of this kind does not amount to property acquisition when a constitutional challenge concerns replacement of a sole management role that carries no beneficial property interest and the former manager participates in the replacement body.

issues.legal_issue: A change to institutional management does not extinguish a person’s separate religious-service rights where the legislation preserves those rights independently of the management role.
material_facts: The challenger’s predecessor held both a management role and a separate position involving religious service and associated rights and privileges.
The legislation ended the sole management role but expressly protected the religious-service rights even if the holder ceased to chair the management body.
Other provisions contemplated that religious-service rights and related entitlements would continue and could be the subject of administrative decisions.
issues.conclusion: The legislation did not take away the challenger’s separate rights and privileges associated with religious service.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished secular management from religious-service status and relied on sections 8, 14, 21(2)(f), 21(2)(g), and 21(3) of the Shri Jagannath Temple Act, 1954. Those provisions showed that service rights and related entitlements remained protected even though the holder’s management role changed. The Court also considered the challenge under Articles 19(1)(f) and 19(5).

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_management_c: A party in a constitutional challenge objects to a change in institutional management.
predicates.religious_service_role_is_separate_from_: The person whose management role changes also holds a distinct role involving religious service.
predicates.legislation_preserves_service_rights_ind: The legislation protects the religious-service rights regardless of whether the person continues to hold the management position.

issues.definition: When a management change is challenged, separate religious-service rights remain unaffected if those rights belong to a distinct role and the legislation preserves them independently of management.

issues.legal_issue: A duty to arrange for the materials and practical support needed for religious services regulates secular administration rather than the religious performance of those services.
material_facts: The management body was required to arrange for the proper performance of services and observances in accordance with an established record of rights.
The Court distinguished providing the materials and practical arrangements for religious services from performing the religious rites themselves.
The legislation left the performance of the religious rites to the persons entitled to perform them.
issues.conclusion: The duty to arrange for the services did not interfere with the religious affairs of the temple.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that religious services have a secular aspect, involving provision of materials and arrangements, and a religious aspect, involving performance of the rites. The challenged duty concerned only the secular aspect and left religious performance untouched. The Court considered the challenge in the context of the Act’s provisions governing temple administration and religious services.

predicates.challenge_to_administrative_duty_for_rel: A party challenges an administrative duty concerning the conduct of religious services.
predicates.duty_concerns_materials_or_practical_arr: The duty concerns providing materials or practical arrangements for the services.
predicates.religious_rites_are_left_to_authorized_p: The persons entitled to perform the religious rites retain responsibility for performing them.

issues.definition: An administrative duty concerning religious services is secular and permissible when it provides materials or practical arrangements while leaving the rites to their authorized performers.

issues.legal_issue: Provisions governing the dissolution or supervision of a management body and the appointment, powers, and discipline of its administrator are valid when they support the lawful management of the institution’s secular affairs.
material_facts: The legislation validly transferred management from a single manager to a committee.

The challenged provisions addressed the committee’s dissolution or supersession, the appointment and duties of an administrator, discipline of staff and service personnel, and governmental supervision.
The Court regarded these provisions as concerning the secular administration of the institution.
issues.conclusion: The challenged provisions concerning the committee and administrator were valid.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that provisions supporting the work of a validly constituted management committee, including provisions for an administrator and supervisory control, could not be attacked on the grounds advanced when they concerned secular management and did not directly affect religious affairs. It considered sections 11, 19, 21, 21A, and 30 of the Shri Jagannath Temple Act, 1954, alongside the constitutional challenges under Articles 19 and 26.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_institutiona: A party challenges the constitutionality of provisions governing administration of a religious institution.
predicates.management_body_is_validly_established: The legislation validly establishes a body to manage the institution.
predicates.challenged_administrative_powers_concern: The challenged powers concern administrative supervision, staffing, or other secular affairs rather than performance of religious rites.

issues.definition: In a constitutional challenge to institutional administration, supporting administrative provisions are valid when the management body is validly established and the powers at issue concern secular affairs.

issues.legal_issue: Constitutional guarantees concerning state support of religion and religious instruction do not apply to legislation dealing with the administrative matters at issue in this case.
material_facts: The legislation dealt with the administration and management of a public religious institution.

The challenger invoked constitutional guarantees concerning state support of religion and religious instruction without showing how those guarantees applied to the matters regulated by the legislation.
issues.conclusion: Articles 27 and 28 had no application to the matters dealt with by the legislation.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that Articles 27 and 28 of the Constitution had nothing to do with the matters dealt with by the Shri Jagannath Temple Act, 1954.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_religious_in: A party raises constitutional objections to legislation administering a religious institution.
predicates.challenged_law_addresses_administrative_: The challenged legislation addresses administration or management rather than state funding of religion or religious instruction.
predicates.no_connection_shown_to_state_religious_s: The challenger does not show a connection between the administrative provisions and state support of religion or religious instruction.

issues.definition: Constitutional guarantees concerning state support of religion or religious instruction do not apply to an administrative law when no connection between that law and those subjects is shown.

issues.legal_issue: A claim that legislation violates a religious denomination’s right to administer property cannot be considered on appeal when the claim was not properly raised in the original proceedings.
material_facts: The original petition did not identify a religious denomination whose administration rights had been affected.
The petition was initially framed on the basis that the challenger owned the temple as private property, and that ownership claim was later abandoned.
A denomination-based argument was advanced before the High Court, but the Supreme Court found that its foundation had not been laid in the petition.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to consider the challenge under Article 26(d) because it had not been properly raised in the High Court.
issues.legal_principle: The Court declined to consider the Article 26(d) claim because the petition did not identify the relevant denomination or properly plead that its rights had been infringed. The Court therefore did not decide the substantive question whether the legislation violated Article 26(d).

predicates.constitutional_appeal: A party appeals a decision in a proceeding challenging the constitutionality of legislation.
predicates.denominational_administration_rights_cla: The party asserts that legislation infringes a religious denomination’s right to administer its property.
predicates.claim_properly_raised_in_original_procee: The party identified the denomination and adequately pleaded the alleged infringement in the original proceedings.

issues.definition: On a constitutional appeal, a denominational administration-rights claim is not considered when it was not properly raised in the original proceedings.
